New York, June 17.—Austro-Hungary offensive against Italy undoubtedly has been ordered by Hindenburg as a final despairing effort to weaken the allies through forcing Italy to withdraw from the war before America's forthcoming offensive can be started.


Hindenburg has taken blind chance at his new blood spilling. BATON ROUGE, La., July 9, 1918
Editor St. Mary Banner:

I have just read a clipping in the Times-Picayune of your recent editorial, which however, was credited to the Watchman, saying "Mr. Gay was selected by myself and Col. Ewing to run against Hall, etc., and that I was an enemy of Sugar & Co.,"

I wish to say that your statement is entirely incorrect. I have already stated several days ago that I knew nothing whatever of Mr. Gay's candidacy until I read same in the press and never once in my life spoke to him about running before his announcement was made.

Now, as to being an enemy of sugar, that is also untrue. I have always advocated tariff on sugar and did so on strictly Democratic and not Republican principles. I still favor such a tariff and believe it will be many years before the issue will be again raised in this country. I have supported many Senators from the Third District and certainly think Mr. Gay ought to be very acceptable to unjudged voters. While Speaker of the House, myself and friends actively supported every measure against the Sugar Trust. Ask Hon. Don Gallery.

It is true, I championed the cause of my friend, Governor Pleasant, who became the Democratic nominee, and I would have supported Governor Barrett in all loyalty had he become the "standard bearer" of the party. There should be nothing personal in our political differences, and with me, there was and is none. If the former Progressives are now back in the Democratic Party because they sincerely believe that party is best, then they certainly have nothing to have against me. Truly yours,

L. E. THOMAS.

Washington, Dec. 16.—Especially a land where highway robbery, murder and other high crimes and misdemeanors are perfectly legal, or at least are not unlawful, will furnish one of the problems that will arise to perplex the peace conference. This land is Spitzbergen, and acts which are punishable by death or imprisonment elsewhere in the world are not unlawful there because there is no law.

For Spitzbergen is in the truest sense of the word a "no man's land," not metaphorically so as was the deadly strip between the front-line trenches in France, but literally what Robert Lansing, Secretary of State, described as terra nullius, a "no man's land," an international freak.

This curiosity among the nations of the earth is not some tiny islet in an isolated corner of the remote seas, but an island, or rather group of islands, of vast extent, embracing 4,000 square miles. Spitzbergen is 400 miles north of Norway, and is about as desolate a place as can be found on the earth's surface. In the few sunny days of midsummer a little grass appears in the sheltered brooks, but for the greater part of the year the Arctic winter reigns supreme.

It would seem that a peace conference that has to settle the myriad questions growing out of the world war would devote precious little time to this group of ice-covered islands in the Arctic ocean, but in the question of their disposition they have set sail on an uncharted sea of international law, for the problem of Spitzbergen is without precedent and without parallel in the history of the world.

Attempt to Steal Spitzbergen.

Germany, before she went out of the business of apportioning the world to suit herself, sought to steal a march on the rest of the nations by inserting a clause in the new defunct Brest-Litovsk treaty dividing the control of Spitzbergen between Germany and Russia; in other words, giving it to Germany. When this clause came to light there was great indignation in England over this act of German presumption. For, until the signing of the Brest-Litovsk treaty neither Germany nor Russia had ever put forth any claim to Spitzbergen. Neither had England, for that matter, nor any other nation. Over Spitzbergen's bleak wastes no flag has ever waved.

The remarkable history of Spitzbergen began when the islands were discovered in 1896 by William Barents, the Dutch explorer. The islands were covered with snow and ice and no one thought to lay claim to such worthless territory. So, while visited occasionally by whalers, they have remained ownerless, through four centuries while the powers of the earth have been scrambling for colonies in fairer lands. But if Spitzbergen is so worthless as to remain unclaimed through all the intervening centuries since Barents entered its harbor, why should the peace conference with its manifold troubles be called upon to add this remote one to its list? The answer is that it has been found that, nesting under Spitzbergen's thick blanket of snow and ice, are great deposits of coal, iron, pure gypsum, marble, and oil-bearing rock.

An American company began the development of coal mines in Spitzbergen about 1900. Other countries hastened to follow suit. Then the curious fact presented itself that Spitzbergen, belonging to no nation, and being without government of any kind, there was no such thing as private right of property there. Conditions as to ownership of property in Spitzbergen were just the same as they were in Europe in the Stone Age, when every man took what he could from his weaker neighbor.

One form of shell food with definite
possibilities for development in this
country is the snail—the savory es-
cargot of France, long an interna-
tional joke, like frog legs, but seldom
failing to make its way with the cul-
ture when fresh and properly pre-
pared. The Department of Agriculture
considers snails important enough to
issue bulletin on snail farming. There
is already a great demand from our
foreign-born population, which would
undoubtedly be increased if snails
were cultivated here. Any back yard
is big enough for snail farm. A plot
5 to 30 feet square will accommodate
10000 snails, fed on leaves, cabbages,
lettuce, endive, chopped kohlrabi, dam-
delion leaves or potatoes. On larger
plots snails will thrive on wild plants.
Snails will not leave their farm if they
have sufficient food and reasonable
range, and do not need to be fenced
in. A female will lay from 30 to 60
eggs in June and July, and in 20 days
the baby snails will be hatched out
and attain marble size by the cold
weather. They spend the winter bur-
ied in the ground, coming out in the
spring and feeding all summer, be-
ing ready for market by the fol-
lowing autumn.—Food Administration
Bulletin.

Under the provisions of the blue sky law every corporation must satisfy the state corporation commission of the good character of the enterprise whose stock is desired to be offered for sale, before such stock can law fully be offered to more than twenty-five persons in this state. The state corporation commission has made ample provision for the administration of this act. Longtime Fighting at the Front


and often Fall Easy Prey to Fresher


and Less Experienced Men-Many


Able Germans Downed-French Lose


Thirteen "Aces."


The autumn of 1917 has been excep-
tionally destructive for the fighting
''aces'' of the warning aviation corps,
many of the greatest and most famous
flyers in both the allied and the enemy
ranks having fallen. A great number
of them had been flying for two and
even three years, and were almost
deemed invincible. 1t is my belief that
after a man has flown and fought at
the front for a long time he becomes
exhausted, and unless he takes a rest,
which few devoted ayiators will con-
sent to do, he falls an easy prey to
some fresher though less experienced
man, writes Paul Ayres Rockwell in
the Chicago Daily News. AT the head
of the list of fallen airmen comes the
glorious Frenchman, Capt. Georges
Guynemer, who had, by official count,
destroyed 90 German airplanes, and
who had surely accounted for at least
twenty others. He was killed in aerial
combat above P%oecapelle, September
II, by the German Lieutenant Wisse-
mann, who was slain a few days later
by Second Lieutenant Fonck. Guyne-
mer was the finest and most romantic
figure this war has yet produced. His
final citation in French army orders
follows:


Georges Guynemer, captain COM
manding escadrille N 3; died on the
field of honor September II, 1917. A
legendary hero, fallen in the full
heaven of glory, after three years of
ardent struggle. Will remain the most
pure example of the qualities of the
race; indomitable tenacity, ~tireless en-
ergy, sublime courage. Animated by
the most unshakable faith in the vic
tory, he bequeaths to the French SOL
der an imperishable souvenir, which
will exalt the spirit of sacrifice and
provoke the most noble emulations."


Another great Frenchman who will
fly no more is Captain Nation, who
shot down nine enemy machines. He
did not return from a flight over the
German lines on September 10. Later
it was learned hat he had been wound
ed, captured and taken to a prison
camp, where he died. These are the
only French "aces' who have been
killed, though several valuable pilots
are no more.


Many Able Germans DoWned.


Now read the long list of German
losses: Capt. Baron Won Richtofen,
commander of the notorious tango
escadrille and credited by the Wolff
communicates with 81 victories, has
been forced by serious wounds to give
up active flying. He was last men
toned in the enemy's communique of
September 3, which chronicled his six
ty-first triumph. Shortly after, he was
reported killed in action, then a British
prisoner. An Amsterdam dispatch Of
October % reported the baron's mar
rage to the daughter of a multimillion-
aire munition maker and stated that
the kaiser had given the noted "ace'
a place on his staff as inspector of all
German aviation schools.


Won Richtofen made his first appear
ance in the enemy communicates on
January "a, 1917, when his seventeenth
victory was chronicled. Why had he
never been spoken of before? Ber-
thOldi's fifth victory, Wintgen's fifth,
Baldann's fourth, Hohndorff's fourth
were cited, the same for Mulzer, LET
fers. Won Althaus and many other
Boche "aces." Yet, although Won
Richtofen was a nobleman, a fact rare
among the German "aces," and in con-
sequence standing an unusually good
chance of being signaled, his debuts
were passed over in silence. Jacques
Mortane, the French aviation writer,
is of the opinion that Won Richtofen's
first IS victories were invented for
him owing to the fact that when he ap-
peared on the scene in the communique
the Boche authorities were sorely in
need of faces" to convince the Ger
man public that their aviation was
superior to that of the allies.


Big Losses in 1917.


Lieut.. Werner Voss Crefeld was
killed September "a, along with his fif-
teenth victim. Lieutenant Gontermann,
who had destroyed 80 allied airplanes
and observation balloons, was killed
accidentally early in November. Lieu
tenant Wolff was slain in an air fight
September Is, after he had triumphed
over SO allied machines. Lieutenant
Dostler, mentioned as having shot down
26 allied airplanes, was killed in COM
bat in mid-November. Lieutenant Ba-
ron Won Richtofen, brother of the noted
captain. vas reported killed by the
British in September. But a later re-
port from Germany indicates that he
was only wounded. He was credited
with t%wenty-four victories. Among his

He has drawn upon the immortal

WASHINGTON. Oct. 30.—Plans for an adjournment of Congress until after election appeared tonight to have been blocked by partisan conflict in the Senate.

Less than a quorum of the Senate is in Washington tonight and Republican leaders said they would exercise their power to prevent the proposed recess, in order that the Senate may discuss any developments in the peace negotiations.

As to the number of class I men that will result from the new registration, assuming that there are about 1000 registrants, it is safe to say that it will not much exceed 500. The government in connection with the registrants of June, 1918, required that at least 50 per cent of them should be placed in Class I. The percentage in Iowa has run higher than that, having nowhere been below 50 per cent, and some boards having placed as high as 75 per cent of these registrants in class I. An average of about 60 per cent, therefore, would probably be a fair estimate.

So far as Iowa is concerned she has not as yet exhausted her quota, or more. Of the 1917 registration there are still between 500 and 900 men, while of the registration on June 5, 1918, there will be a shortage when classification is fully completed. As has been the case in other states however, so in Iowa the work of classifying the June, 1918, registrants has been unaccountably delayed, although it is now nearing completion. Very few of the June 5 registrants have as yet been classified. In some instances the local boards were compelled to call on them to make up the shortage of 170 men in the call for 3,265 men that went to Camp Forrest, Ga., on July 20. There were also few 1918 registrants among the 500 Aug. 5.

Quotas Sent Out.

The calls for Iowa men thus far in August have not resulted in the withdrawal of more than 1,890 men. They are as follows:

Aug. 5, 500 men to Jefferson Barracks, Mo.; Aug. 11, 2 physicians to Jefferson Barracks; Aug. 15, 500 men to Ames college for training in auto mechanics; Aug. 22, 50 Negroes to Camp Dodge; Aug. 26, 500 men to Camp Funston, KAN; Aug. 30, 150 limited service men to Camp Dodge.

Information was given out by the provost marshal general that the August calls would be equal to those of July, which aggregated about 1,900 men. As already stated, however, the calls have been held up owing to delays in classification. A request is now out, however, asking for the number of available class I men by Aug. 15, on the basis of which report it is expected that a call will be issued that will probably take most of the class I men in the state.

New York.—The Western Union Telegraph Company has declined to submit to the jurisdiction of the national war labor board which sought to adjust the differences between the company and those of its employees who are members of the Commercial Telegraphers' Union of America.


The Western Union's decision became known when the report of the executive session of the war board was made public. It embodied a report by W. H. Taft and Frank P. Walsh, joint chairmen of the board, who conferred with Newcomb Carlton, president of the Western Union, in an effort to compose the differences between the company and those of its employees who had been discharged because they joined the Commercial Telegraphers' Union of America.


Complaint against the company's action was taken to the war board and Mr. Taft and Mr. Walsh made an investigation. They then submitted a proposition in the nature of compromise based on the principles of the work of the war board. This platform recognizes the right of men to organize and holds they shall not be discharged for membership in trades unions or for legitimate trade union activities.


"The Western Union is not seeking to deprive any one of his inalienable rights," said Mr. Carlton in a statement issued, "but it recognizes that its employees must choose employment with it or membership in the C. T. U. of A., with employment in the many other telegraph positions open to them, for the Western Union employs less than 20 per cent of the total telegraphers in the United States.


If you desire to join the C. T. U. of A., then we must part. So long as you retain your position with the company you will have every protection and full right of appeal, but we cannot agree that you shall join any organization which imperils the continuity of the telegraph service which this company is expected to provide for the government and public of the United States."


Mr. Taft and Mr. Walsh, their report showed, recommended to Mr. Carlton that the Western Union receive a committee of its own men only, who desired to present requests for better working conditions or compensation, and if an agreement could not be reached, the matter should be referred to the war board and the question disposed of according to its rules.

There will be no dancing class this winter as in former years; interpretative folk and character dancing have been done away with and replaced by system of military drill. The work in military tactics and drill requires four hours a week at the most, three at the least. With the French Armies. June 8.

During the last three days I have visited the Marne front from Dormans to Chateau-Thierry and watched the resistance stiffening. Tempted as the enemy must be to essay a drive across the river, it is doubtful whether he will risk the attempt. The name of the Marne rings like a tocsin in the ears of every Frenchman, and the poilus will fight to the death to keep the river as final barrier.

The operations in this region are entirely open warfare, such as Americans knew in the Civil War. Save for an occasional airplane buzzing overhead, the observer might be watching a reproduction of one of the battle stories of Ambrose Bierce. Here a battery position at the edge of a wood. A little further machine guns are installed to sweep the river bank and among the trees behind them a battalion of infantry is under cover. Patrols of cavalry move swiftly from point to point, and on a hillside opposite a German convoy, in full view of the naked eye, is dashing along a stretch of open road under fire of French guns.

On the heights to the left sudden smoke clouds leap up incessantly where the shells are obstructing the advance of the German infantry near Chateau-Thierry. From time to time one catches sight of them scurrying forward like ants across an interval of meadows between the woods that cover most of the country. The war clock has been put back forty years, and along the whole front of action the position of deadlock has given place to battle of movement. There is no time now to prepare trenches and barbed wire and miles of elaborate camouflage. The decisive struggle of the war will be fought out by maneuver as of old.

Great Battle Analysed

An analysis of the great battle has been given to your correspondent. The British line on May 31 ran from a point west of Craonne to Bemery court. While naturally dealing chiefly with British participation, the account is sufficiently general to enable one to realize the progress of events and their bearing on the present situation. On the night of May 31 prisoners were captured by the French on the British left. They vouched for the information that a great attack was planned for the following night. To all appearances there seemed reason to question the accuracy of this information.

Owing to the bad weather, aerial photography had been of limited use in locating the enemy batteries, but as far as could be ascertained their number was not abnormal. Nevertheless, on the night of May 31 orders were given to the French Army, of which the British division formed a part, that all the Allied corps should take up battle positions. At midnight counter-preparation was opened with every available gun. The Germans began an hour later according to schedule, and the volume of fire was such that the trenches, batteries, local headquarters, and all points of concentration and communication were literally smothered in gas and high explosives.

Against the three British divisions—the Fiftieth on the left, the Eighth in the center, and the Twenty-first on the right, all of which had been engaged in the previous battles—the Germans launched their storm divisions, with divisions in support which came into action almost immediately.

On the French front the odds were considerably greater. The Fiftieth suddenly discovered the enemy in strong force behind their left brigade, which was enveloped. The Germans rapidly widened the gap on both sides, and by noon the defenders were established on the new line, south of the Aisne.

Flushed by their recent success, the Germans forced the passage of the river, driving through to Guyencourt. The pressure on the British Fiftieth and Eighth divisions had been heavy.

During Tuesday and Wednesday the enemy advanced along the whole front, sparing no effort and disregarding all losses. The boche fought magnificently—is the generous tribute the British pay to their opponents.

On Wednesday evening the Allied line was a semicircle from Loupeigne through Couionges and Lagesy to the River Vesle at Muizon.

As before stated, the retreat was orderly in that defenders were able to remain in touch after each falling back, but the enemy invariably took advantage of their superior numbers to break through weak points and compel the withdrawal of adjacent units to "infiltration" under menace of envelopment.

From that date their lines remained fairly stable. They were reinforced on Thursday morning and simply withdrew in step with the center, where German pressure henceforth was heaviest.

The enemy may attempt the passage of the river, but his success is extremely doubtful, and in any case, his principal effort is now being directed westward against the flank of the main Allied forces.

The enemy is now exerting his full strength—more than fifty divisions already have been identified—in a southwestward direction. He is doing his utmost to increase his gains in the angle of the new bulge around Scissors and further south toward the forest of Villers-Cotterêts in order to keep an alignment with the principal push through the Ourcq Valley by Neuilly en Front in the direction of Paris.

According to latest news, the Allied stance is of steel, and there have been many successful counter-attacks. On the front, from west of Scissors to the Marne, the Allies are standing at bay.

the growing shortage OF physicians,
the passage through the city of large
numbers of soldiers and sailors, many

How can the Germanized government of the dual empire compel its people to make the appalling sacrifices which are entailed by such a situation?

The eastern frontier of Austria is open to an immediate attack from Serbia with Bulgaria disposed of and Turkey flat on her back. The powerful and victorious allied army in Macedonia has turned upon the Austrians still in Albania and, after overwhelming or driving them back to their own frontier, will throw itself across the Danube for a thrust at the very heart of Austria.

Then there is Roumania, simmering under the outrageous peace terms forced upon her by the Bucharest treaty. She is now girding herself for a fresh effort to throw off the yoke which the central powers laid upon her; to recover her Black Sea possessions ruthlessly taken from her; to reclaim her lands which were seized when Austria receded her western frontier. With contact restored with the allies through the creation of Serbia, Roumania doubtless will jump at the chance to plunge again at the throat of Austria.

Once more there is the reorganized Italian army on the Piave standing ready to spring at the Austro-Hungarian forces now entrenched upon Italian soil. All General Diaz wants is word from Marshal Foch to start his offensive, and when the Italian commander moves this time, he will move with the determination to annihilate the enemy before him. Thus surrounded by hostile forces, rent at home by Czecho-Slovak and Jugo-Slav revolt and unable to command German reinforcements, the position of Austria is serious.

With the British Army on the St. Quentin Sector, Oct. 3.—The British troops smashed a large and vital section of the Hindenburg line to-day between St. Quentin and Cambrai. They have occupied many additional towns and villages and 5000 prisoners and numerous guns have been taken.

The battle was resumed at 6 o'clock in the morning and continued throughout the day, English and Australian divisions driving deep into the enemy defenses. The ground over which the British troops fought their way against the inevitable swarms of machine guns was littered with German dead.

The advance has reached a depth of about FIVE miles at its apex, and it follows that the principal Hindenburg defenses here have been shattered. A few hours may see the British all the way on the other side of the great German defensive system.

From the north comes most significant news. The Germans, who were gradually being left in a salient, have begun a retreat on practically all the Armentieres sector and appear to be in full flight. British troops have entered and are now passing through Lens.

Aubers ridge, south of Armentieres, has been taken, and the British are east of there. Indications are not wanting that the Germans have been forced to begin one of the war's greatest retreats. The troops cooperating with the Belgians have taken villages near Roulers after hard street fighting.

Mr. Browne has kept in close touch with the mining situation, and said that full advantage should be taken of the fact that Nenana is the divisional headquarters for the government railroad and is also situated in the heart of a highly mineralized belt, embracing the Kantishna, Tanana, Hot Springs, Panama, Kuskokwim and other districts, and that full advantage should be taken of this also to boost for the smelter. With the establishment of the smelter, important industries of permanent character are bound to spring up, in furthering Nenana's future greatness. Concerted action was the keynote of Mr. Browne's remarks, and action, he said, should not be delayed a moment. Nenana's opportunity is at hand. "If I can be a knocker," said Mr. Browne, whose whole-hearted support in any project with the development of the country's resources as the object in view, can always be counted on.

It is the intention of the government, Mr. Browne said, to control public utilities for the public welfare, and the way they have administered the affairs of such public utilities in the States as the railroads, telegraph, cable and radio service, etc. has demonstrated the fact that the public who are affected by these utilities are much better served and derive more benefit from them. A government-owned or government-controlled smelter would be the proper thing for the Interior, he said, and a square deal in the matter of rates can then be calculated on. The present administration is very friendly to Alaska, and the country has no greater friend than Secretary of the Interior Lane who is ever ready to listen to any reasonable proposition that would benefit the Northland.

Coal, lime, silica and the other materials that are needed for the successful operation of a smelter can be obtained in abundance in this district, and in the nearby mining districts, and it is up to the progressive spirits here to dig up the evidence of this and lay it before the proper authorities at Washington, with a request for smelter, and good is bound to result.

Powerful opposition from the big interests will be encountered, he said, and the effort put forth by Nenanaites must be steady and persistent. Temporary setbacks, failures and disappointments should not be allowed to interfere with the efforts put forth. These things may be disheartening, but they are not insurmountable and, he thought, the Commercial Club, with a united Nenana to back its effort, should be able eventually to secure government smelter, the establishing of which will herald the dawn of big things for Interior Alaska in general and Nenana in particular. — Nenana News.

The League has drawn up a comprehensive plan, which will be put in operation in every state in the Union under the direction of "Committee on Preliminary Training and Instruction of Men Registered for Draft" of which Surgeon General Charles R. Stokes, U. S. N., retired, is chairman.


Crowder Approves.


Provost Marshal General Crowder, to whom the Security League submitted the idea before acting, has approved it in a letter to Col. Charles Q. Lydecker, President of the League, in which he says:


"Your proposal gives me great satisfaction. Your League can render valuable assistance in this manner."


The Security League's plan will be made effective through the 281 branches of the League, scattered in all parts of the country, and subcommittee of Surgeon General Stokes's committee cooperating with the Local Draft Boards in all the states. It provides for the organization into instruction classes of the men soon to be called, to be selected by the Draft Boards, the actual training to be conducted by retired or disabled army officers, whose efforts to prepare the young men for service will be supplemented by local clergymen and physicians.


Gen. J. Franklin Bell, commandant at Camp Upton, is an enthusiastic supporter of the plan and has promised the Security League cooperation in obtaining instructors for the classes in New York City and vicinity.


"Clean, Sober Soldiers"


"The object of our endeavor will be to make the young men understand why they are called for service to their country, what is to be expected of them and why they should be loyal, clean, sober and intelligent soldiers," says Surgeon General Stokes. Outlining the operation of the plan, he continues:


"There are three main working points:


(1) Each Local Draft Board, through its Chairman, will select a Captain, who will procure the assembly of the registrants and obtain from local military or naval post, State Guard or Home Defense Unit or from retired or disabled veterans of the present war an adequate training officer.


(2) The Captain will also invite a local clergyman to give information, instruction and advice to the young men.


Save Time and Money.


(3) A local physician will also instruct the young men in matters of health, hygiene and physical well-being in order that when they go to camp they shall present themselves with a consciousness of knowledge which will add to their strength and usefulness.


At present the vast majority of our young men are called to the colors untrained. It would greatly facilitate their being turned into soldiers and save the government time and money if when they are called they are provided with some knowledge of military training and a sense of discipline and organization.


The position of local Captain, who will supervise the work, offers one of the finest opportunities for patriotic service for men of standing in the community who are unable to get into the trenches.


"Disorganized Rabble"


Under the guidance of such a man aided by an influential local clergyman and physician, the drafted men will go to their environments in efficient, organized bodies rather than as disorganized rabble and with spirit of self-reliance and comradeship. All the strangeness of the new life will have been eliminated, and, since the men will have been taught what lies before them, they will face duty with the confidence of familiarity.


The military instruction will comprise only the simplest evolutions, with particular emphasis upon military courtesy—when, where, how and whom to salute. A general supervision of this phase of the training for uniformity and efficiency will be conducted by the government military authorities. Armories, public parks and squares, public school fairgrounds, etc., will be utilized for the actual drilling. Drills two or three times a week of an hour's duration will be preferable to longer periods at less frequent intervals.


Fitted for Officers.


Competitive drills will be arranged to stimulate interest and enthusiasm. One of the advantages of the plan will be that the men who prove most proficient in the preliminary training will have an excellent chance of being selected.

Washington, Jan. 7—Approximately 400 passenger trains have been taken off the three principal railroads operating east of Pittsburgh, according to announcement made at the office of Director General McAdoo.

The Pennsylvania system has dropped more than 125 passenger trains; the New Haven 81; the Baltimore & Ohio, 60; the New York Central, 50; and other roads varying numbers from 5 to 25, according to the character of their service. Some of the others which are curtailed greatly are the Philadelphia & Reading, the Erie, the Delaware & Hudson, the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western, the New York, Ontario & Western, the Boston & Maine, and the Boston & Albany.

These were all parlor car trains, or trains of chair cars. Locomotives relieved by the cutting off of these trains will be turned to the hauling of coal and generally relieving the freight congestion.

No more passenger trains will be cut off in the immediate future; but the Director General may make a further cutting in the number of cars allotted to some trains.

New Demurrage Rules.

Director General McAdoo last night made public the demurrage rules, regulations and charges.

1. Forty-eight hours free time for loading or unloading on all commodities.

2. Twenty-four hours free time on cars held for any other purpose permitted by tariff.

3. Demurrage charges per car per day or fraction of a day car is released as follows: $5 for the first day; $1 for the second day, and for each succeeding additional day charge is to be increased $5 in excess of that for the preceding day until a maximum charge of $40 per car per day shall be reached the eighth day of detention beyond free time; the charge thereafter to be $40 per car per day or fraction thereof.

These charges will supersede all those named in existing tariffs applicable to domestic freight, and specially contemplate the cancellation of all average agreement provisions of existing tariffs.

Special Dispatch to Public Ledger
Camp Meade, Md., Nov. 1.

Twenty thousand and more men wearing the swagger little fatigue caps which are worn by the Americans abroad passed in review here today before Major General Carter, commander of the Lafayette Division, and by other high officers of the camp.

It was the most novel and picturesque review ever held in this cantonment. It was worth going many miles to see these men, all fit and ready for the fray, looking just as they will look if ever they are called upon to go to France. The men of the Lafayette Division have about finished their training on this side of the ocean. They are eager to do their bit, but every officer and man in the crowd wondered this morning whether or not he would ever be given chance to get over.

Many of the officers in the parade have had their chance. These officers wore on the left sleeve of their uniforms one or two gold chevrons, indicating their months of service in the war zone, and some of them wore on their right arms the proud wound chevrons. Few of them had on decorations received for gallantry in action.

Brigadier General S. J. Bayard Schindel, commander of the Twenty-first Infantry Brigade, commanded the parade. General Schindel is Pennsylvanian.

There were many visitors from Washington present. All in all, with the soldiers marching and the bands playing, the affair was one to set the patriotic chords jumping. The review took more than two hours. Immediately after the review all the bands in the camp hurried to Baltimore to take part in the big united war drive parade to be held in that city this afternoon.

Officers Win Promotions

Forty-one officers of this camp have been made very happy through the receipt of the news of their promotion. Of this number seventeen were promoted from first lieutenancies to captaincies and twenty-four from second lieutenancies to first lieutenancies. Those named captains were:

John R. Gaut, Samuel O'Keefe, William E. Ashford, Dexter Bush, James C. Pagan, William S. Hazlet, Bethel A. Simmons, Manly Q. Thompson, Daniel R. McMullen, Joseph G. Matthews, Barrett Prettyman, Alfred Reed, Charles L. Robinson, Kirkwood H. Scott, Thomas Y. Sullivan, Edward S. Vaughn and Marshall Low.

Those who have been promoted to first lieutenancies are: John N. Allen, William H. Althaus, Harvey T. Bennett, Francis C. Beverley, William H. Blanchard, Scott A. Burnam, William J. Bushwaller, Charles W. Camp, Wesley L. Cary, A. R. Clancy, Irwin J. Charbonnet, Edward U. Chase, John W. Cochran, Hess C. Florida, George H. Moore, Frank J. Prochaska, Elmer H. Ranker, Harry J. Schaffer, Craig F. Sears, Dot F. Smith, John A. Stanley, John L. Strode, Roger Stefan and Lucian N. Totaro.

Lieutenant Bethel A. Simmons, one of those promoted to captain, has been for the last month or more the head of the noncoms training school in camp. His work at the camp has been so good that it was known that it was only a question of time regarding his promotion.

Many of the officers named are Pennsylvanians. A number of the new captains who are native sons of the Keystone State came here as second lieutenants. These men were made first lieutenants some months ago. All of these officers are in the Depot Brigade.

A big crowd is expected tomorrow to attend the two memorial services which are to be held for the men in this camp who died from influenza. A memorial mass at which Cardinal Gibbons will preside will be celebrated by Lieutenant Michael Y. Fogarty, Catholic chaplain, of the Seventeenth Regiment. Lieutenant Daniel H. Desmond will preach the sermon. The music of the mass will be sung by the choir of St. Mary's Seminary, Baltimore. The 154th depot brigade band will play. A guard of honor to escort the Cardinal and other officers of the mass to the altar will be composed of members of the foreign legion of the development battalion, this battalion comprising representatives of a couple of dozen or more countries. The names of the men who died in the epidemic will be placed on the altar during the services. Remembrance will be made in the mass to all Meade men who have died in France.

A nondenominational memorial service will be held at the same time in the Y. M. C. A. section of the camp. It will be in charge of Lieutenant Byron Hester, one of the Protestant chaplains. There will be singing of hymns, reading of Scriptures, a sermon and special prayer offered. The development band will play and the whole ceremony will be most impressive.

Chicago, Feb. 10. Witnesses testified at the meat packers wage arbitration hearing before Federal Judge Schuler today that the life of stock yards laborers who reside in the district known as back of the yards is a bitter struggle for existence.

Mrs. Rosalie Bobek, a widow of 10 days and the mother of three children, said her husband worked for Wilson & Co. in the yards several years before he died as the result of falling down stairs at home. She carried her 3-year-old boy to the witness stand with her and gazed at the arbitrator through tear-dimmed eyes as she told her story with the aid of an interpreter.

From $8 to $40 a week

The woman said her husband earned from $8 to $40 a week when he first went to work in the killing department of Wilson & Co. Later he was promoted to wheeling truck on the loading platform and earned more, but never lived. He died when he worked 80 hours and received $50.

When her children had measles she did not have money enough to have a doctor and when her husband died she had to rely on friends to pay his funeral expenses, she testified. In answer to questions by Attorney Frank J. Walsh, she said she had no new clothes, no picnic or other form of amusement; had lived back of the yards. She said she never even went for street car rides to public parks because she could not afford it.

"Can't you ever go to Lincoln Park and see the statues of Abraham Lincoln, George Washington and Henry Clay?" asked Attorney Walsh.

"No," she answered. "I always stay at home because I had no money to go out."

Never Saw Lake Michigan

"Did you ever see Lake Michigan?"

"No."

"How long have you been in Chicago?"

"Six years."

She testified that her husband never earned enough money in the stock yards to clothe and feed the family.

The work of the hospital searcher is varied. Of course her chief work is in finding missing men who seem to be lost, then there are a thousand and one things to be done for the soldiers that the nurses do not have time to do and these duties fall to the lot of the searcher. She must write letters to mothers, wives and sweethearts, for the soldiers in the hospital who are not able to do so for themselves. "It feels that I have written to every sweetheart in America," said Miss Francis yesterday. She also related two incidents of cases where the soldiers had lost limbs. In the letters of one who had lost his right arm she had to keep the fact that he was cripple for life from his wife, as he said he was not going to tell her until he got home. Richmond, Nov. 1.—On account of the disrupted conditions of work and the great amount of time lost because of the influenza epidemic, the annual meeting of the Virginia Education Conference will not be held Thanksgiving week.

Question of holding the conference during the Christmas holidays or at a later date in the spring, or the decision not to have a conference this school year, was deferred until after the meeting of the executive committee of the State Teachers Association, which will be held in two weeks.

Owing to the time lost on account of the influenza epidemic, two questions will occur to schools: first, the effect of the term reduction on the credit and standing of schools; second, the advisability of teaching Saturdays and, on other days, in order to compensate for time lost.

On the first question: the State Department of Education rules that all arrangements have been made for a nine months term, the teachers are paid for the time, and reasonable care is taken to compensate partially for the handicaps to pupils because of loss of time, the credit of a school which, in the circumstances, maintains term somewhat less than nine months need not be lowered. In regard to the second proposition, the department suggests that, rather than each Saturday, the following program may enable school officials to make up a considerable portion of time lost: "Save two days Thanksgiving" it says, "by teaching both Wednesday and Friday, reserving a portion of Thursday for appropriate exercises. Save about five days at Christmas by giving a holiday one week in length, namely, from December 15 to December 20, inclusive. Two days saved on the birthdays of Lee and Washington, in as much as one is Sunday and the other Saturday.

For schools which give more than one day at Easter, the holiday should be reduced to one day. Save three or four days at end of the session by having commencement exercises exclusive of the regular school term by reducing the time devoted to examinations. In addition to the above, one or two days may be saved by teaching one or two Saturdays or by extending the term one or two days. The above schedule for the average division will save approximately thirteen school days or three weeks."

ers of eastern Washington has been

part in war activities is asked to send
delegates to the meetings. There is
no limit to the number of delegates

prime purpose is to discuss the var
ious problems incident to war activi-

plans for general furtherance of the

the Davenport hotel. A general
luncheon will follow. The afternoon
will be given over to the general con-
ference. In the evening public mass
meeting will be held at the armory.

meetings and at the same time the
commercial bodies will hold their con-
vention. A patriotic luncheon will be
held at the chamber Of commerce with
all visitors as guests Of honor. The
concluding session of the general con-
ference will be held in the afternoon.

the mass meeting and also at the var
ious sectional assemblies. They are
George B. Chandler and James A. B.

National Council of Defense; Lieuten-
ant Paul Perigord, special represen-
tative of the French government who
has seen three years of active service,
and Guy Stanton Ford, of Washington,

committee on public information.

An appeal to President Wilson to speed up governmental machinery in aid of production so as to relieve the anxiety of farmers as to labor supply, credit facilities and seed shortage, was made today in a memorial from the federal board of farm organizations in behalf of more than 2,000,000 organized farmers.


The board asked for a reply February 11, when representatives of the seven national farm organizations comprising the board, together with a number of state masters of agriculture and heads of the society of equity and other bodies will seek an audience with the president to discuss constructive plans. The memorial said:


"Food is to win the war. We are assured on every side. The farmers of America must produce more food in 1919 than they did in 1917, but unless present conditions are radically changed, increased crops next year are impossible. Millions of acres will be wholly or partly idle next summer because the money to buy seed and supplies will be lacking. Many of the farmers thus affected are tenants whom misfortune will compel to abandon the farm.


So far as we have learned there is not a single genuine farmer, representative of the organized farmers of America, in any position of authority in the food administration, the advisory council of national defense, or any of the other special boards charged with the conduct of the war.

That Van Sicklin will not withdraw from the race in favor of Martin is certain. Mr. Van Sicklin has issued the following statement which has been received by Latah county democrats.

"A deal in Idaho politics unexampled in its exhibition of nerve and raw assumption of authority to speak for the democrats of the state is being engineered from the state house by Frank Martin, himself a candidate for the democratic nomination for governor. Martin has evidently [convinced] these chair-warmers a continuation of their pull at the public treasury and both himself and his followers have lost their sense of the decencies, of partizan politics."

Mr. Van Sicklin has sent here a copy of telegram he has sent to the Boise committee which asked him to withdraw from the race. The telegram follows:

"Replying to your night letter received this morning will say that I have been and am being importuned by leading democrats all over the state who have the welfare of the party at heart to remain in the race. I and my supporters concede the right of Frank Martin or any other democrat to contest in the primary and ask the same privilege for myself. E. A. Van Sicklin."

Samuels, indorsed by the nonpartisan league, Frank Martin, indorsed by Governor Alexander, and Van Sicklin.

became one of the favorites of the
young empress whose bitter enemy
he was to show himself later on
and, thanks to her, he was induced
to become attentive to the great
charm of the sister of his own sis-
ter-in-law, the Duchess Stana of
Leuchtenberg, one of the beautiful
daughters of the king of Monte
negro. The empress wished him to
marry her and did not care in the
least for any claims that the for-
mer Madame Bourenine might have
upon the grand duke. She caused
it to be conveyed to the lady that
the fact of her existence at the side
of the grand duke could only prove
an impediment to his future career
and political and military activity
and she worked so well upon the
feelings of the poor woman who had
really and faithfully loved Nicholas
Nicholaiewitsch that she decided to
sacrifice herself to his welfare and
applied in her turn for the annul-
ment of the secret marriage which
had bound her to him. She did this
simply and nobly, and the grand
duke accepted this sacrifice much
to the revolt and the disgust of
those who knew them both.


Very soon he married the Duchess
Stana, whilst his former wife, and
that of the children she had given
to him, whose future he assured in
an ample manner, retired to an es-
tate she had acquired in the Crimea,
where most probably she is still liv-
ing.

HARRISBURG, Penn., March 15.—Persons were killed and twenty-six injured early to-day when a boulder weighing about 800 tons crashed into the Cincinnati, Indianapolis and Chicago express on the Pennsylvania railroad in the Elizabethtown cut, about nineteen miles east of here. The train had left New York City at 3.50 P. M. Thursday night and several residents of New York City were hurt.

Miss Rena Palmer, of Morgantown, W. Va., was crushed to death in a sleeping car in which Miss Vera Ravenscroft, of Pittsburgh, was fatally injured, dying on a relief train sent from this city.

The immense boulder slid down the bank and wrecked three sleepers, the third, fourth and fifth cars from the front end of the train. The rock was twenty-four feet long, twelve feet wide and eight feet thick and had to be blasted later before it could be removed.

Almost as soon as news of the wreck was received, relief trains were sent from here and from Lancaster. A number of soldiers who were on the train gave first aid to the injured, while troops stationed near the scene of the wreck rushed to the spot in motor trucks.
